fact: The first electric vehicle was built in the 1800s. Scottish inventor Robert Anderson developed the first crude electric carriage between 1832 and 1839.
EV motors are incredibly simple compared to internal combustion engines. They can have fewer moving parts, which results in significantly lower maintenance needs.
Many electric cars can go from 0 to 60 mph in under 5 seconds, allowing for instant torque and rapid acceleration.
EVs use regenerative braking. When you lift your foot off the accelerator, the motor acts as a generator, converting kinetic energy into electricity to recharge the battery.
Because electric cars are exceptionally quiet, many countries legally require them to emit artificial noises at low speeds to alert pedestrians of their approach.
Early EVs had very short ranges. A locomotive built in 1842 could only travel 1.5 miles on a single charge, whereas modern EVs can easily exceed 400 miles.
China and Norway are global leaders in EV adoption, with the former producing the majority of the world's electric vehicles and batteries.
EV batteries can often find a second life. Instead of being discarded, they are frequently repurposed for large-scale, stationary grid storage before being fully recycled.
